articles.text: Staff moves forward with plans to create 587 new housing units by 2031 The city will not pursue an appeal to decrease the number of housing units mandated by state housing law. Instead, city staff were directed to move forward with plans to create over 500 new and fairly-priced units by the end of 2031. On Monday, June 21, City Council considered an appeal of the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) that has been assigned to Piedmont. RHNA quantifies the need for housing within each jurisdiction across the state during specified planning periods. The next mandated RHNA requires that Piedmont produce 587 new homes and apartments at fair pricing by the year 2031, the end of the next RHNA cycle. The expected allocation includes 163 very low-income units, 94 low-income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above-moderate income units. “Instead of appealing [the city’s mandated] RHNA, Piedmont can show leadership by embracing the effort to meet the housing needs of the Bay Area,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson told councilmembers. Piedmont is challenged by its built-out quality; with very little space to create new housing units, the city and its residents have largely considered accessory dwelling units (ADUs) as a way to fulfill the current RHNA. The city is close to meeting, and surpassing, the amount of housing units mandated by the current RHNA 2015-2023, or 5th RHNA cycle, according to a 2020 annual progress report. Piedmont has issued building permits for the construction of over 70 new units out of a mandated 60 units by the end of next year, 2022. On May 3, city council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting, Inc., (LWC) to prepare updates to the city’s housing element. LWC submitted the only proposal received. In addition, City Attorney Michelle Kenyon advised councilmembers that an appeal would likely not succeed and that the expense of pursing an appeal of the 2023 - 2031 RHNA is not worth it. According to Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell, appeals by cities in Southern California were only partially successful in reducing their allocations. “I’m all for ambitious goals, and I fully appreciate that appealing our RHNA allocation is not a good use of our time and resources, that can be better spent thinking about how we will meet those ambitious goals,” Councilmember Betsy Andersen said.
articles.title: City will not appeal State housing mandate

articles.text: Editor: Recent letters to the Piedmont Post from Shirley Hooi voicing concerns over education content in the public schools show her to be a responsible, concerned parent that wants the best education for her children. The phrase “critical race theory” has appeared in the media as it relates to public education, and it has her worried. A simple media search that you can do will provide, as it did for me, a clear explanation of this phrase and how it is being used. Here is what I found. You should be able to easily find the same in the media and on the internet: 1. Critical race theory (CRT) is an intellectual “framework” used by university and graduate schools as a “tool” to aid in discussions revolving around the role that race has in a culture. These discussions have been going on since the mid- 1990’s. 2. CRT is not the title of a curriculum or a class (like History or English). 3. CRT cannot by its nature as a “framework” be taught in public schools in California. 4. It seems that Ms. Hooi has been told an alternate definition of CRT that is false. 5. This false definition is another dangerous example of a type of propaganda that distorts a word or phrase or slogan and creates a new false meaning that aligns with the false belief system of a group or political party that does the distortioning. In this case it is a simple matter to go on the internet and satisfy yourself of the truth (or falsehood) of what I have said. Beyond CRT, she indicates concern that guilt over racial issues come down on her children. This is understandable and brings up the recurring issue of what and when do we expose our children to difficult issues in the real world. I believe our children are tougher than we think. School presents in its best form a neutral, non-threatening environment to present issues and facts to students. The creation of fully functioning future citizens of our country requires that they receive the knowledge to be active members of our society. History, Social studies, Government, Environment must be taught in the schools. Reading, Writing and Arithmetic are not enough. I admire Ms. Hooi for taking the trouble to express her concerns in this forum. It is parents like her that create the excellent school district in Piedmont. –Alan Rudy
articles.title: Observations of Critical Race Theory

articles.text: A colleague and I were recently called upon to minister to a family after the tragic death of their child. I do not know of a pain greater than the death of a child. I do not know of a loss more heartbreaking. The family’s counselor had recommended the book Bearing the Unbearable: Love, Loss and the Heartbreaking Path of Grief by Joanne Cacciatore to them. The title accurately describes what they are being asked to do, to bear the unbearable. Tragedies like the death of a child bring questions like “Why?”, “Where was God?”, and “Is this truly God’s will?” to the fore. One could spend a lifetime reasoning, researching, praying, studying, discerning in an attempt to answer these questions, and still fall short of any semblance of understanding. I know that, for me, satisfactory answers have yet to present themselves. Rather than answers, what I find are promises like this from I Corinthians 13. Now faith, hope and love remain – these three things – and the greatest of these is love. The Bible Points from this year’s Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church Vacation Bible Camp are in the same vein. articles.text: Piedmont Police officer Jason Germano assisted Oakland police officers in rescuing a man and dog from a burning car on the city border on June 15. Officer Germano was on patrol when he heard on his radio that Oakland police needed help from someone with a fire extinguisher. A car was engulfed in flames at the intersection of Park Boulevard and Estates Drive on the Oakland-Piedmont border, and someone was still inside the vehicle. Germano arrived at the scene at about 11:20 p.m. “I grabbed my extinguisher from my vehicle and sprayed the front of the [crashed] car but wasn’t able to put the fire out,” he explained. Germano, an auto mechanic for over 20 years prior to joining the Police Department in 2019, said he understood that he had “limited time to act.” The driver initially refused to come out of the vehicle and appeared incoherent. Body camera footage shows Germano pulling the man out with the help of Oakland police officers. An OakBody camera footage shows the hood of the car engulfed in flames. Officer Jason Germano land officer then safely pulled the dog out of the burning vehicle. The scene was turned over to the Oakland Police Department for further investigation, and alcohol impairment is a suspected factor in the collision. It is unclear how the fire started, but body camera footage shows the vehicle facing the wrong way on Park Boulevard adjacent to yellow safety poles along the street. “The driver was transported to a local hospital for medical treatment,” Oakland Police Department confirmed in a statement. “The quick actions of all the officers saved the life of the driver and dog.”
articles.title: PPD Officer Jason Germano saves man, dog from burning car

articles.text: Constantly adapting and finding ways to make things happen, the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) will continue hosting the city’s traditional July 4 Pancake Breakfast. Instead of having it at the Veterans Hall, it will be held outdoors on Waldo Avenue from 9 a.m. to 12 noon this Sunday, July 4. Each year the coed teen crew cooks and serves a sumptuous pancake breakfast to hundreds of residents as a fundraiser that helps support the extensive community volunteer work by the crew. The outdoor event is open to the public and will be a bona fide block party on the block-long street, located just off Highland Avenue. Pancakes, Aidells sausages, fresh fruit, coffee and juice will be served, courtesy of donated products from Piedmont Grocery, Starbucks, and Village Market. Cooks and servers will be fully vaccinated and wearing masks and gloves. Arts and crafts and other kid-friendly games will be provided. Families may order tickets for the whole family ahead of time or buy on Sunday on Waldo Avenue. Tickets are $15 for people age 14 and older, and $10 for children. Advance tickets may be purchased at: https://forms.gle/1LwsoZK3peDycnZq5.

articles.text: Editor: I have worked with our Superintendent for the last several years as part of the Steering Committee for the new STEM and performing arts building projects funded by the Measure H1 bond program. Reporting to the School Board, he has the ultimate charge of ensuring that the bond delivers what was promised to our community. I am a retired high-tech executive. From my experience he is an outstanding administrator, very skilled and knowledgeable within the California Public Education System. I am very impressed with the quality of the PUSD staff that he was able to attract to the project. By the way he delegated responsibilities and leveraged their domain knowledge while still keeping the helm. He has outstanding communication skills adapted to the many constituents within the District and the community. His decisions were always guided by consulting teachers and students, the future customers of these new facilities. He is a clear thinker able to synthesize problems to their core, thereby setting paths for solution. The “four scandals” mentioned by Jodi Biskup in her opinion published in last week’s edition of the Post raise two questions: Who has primary responsibility for the moral education of our children: parents or the School District? To what extent is the power of the Superintendent constrained by law and the California Education Code? As a Piedmont homeowner since 1984 and having lived through several school administrations, I encourage you to support our Superintendent. We have a great school district that serves our many constituents well. –Bernard Pech For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Applications due by July 9 The city is seeking volunteers to help complete a recycling audit of waste bins. Volunteers will conduct field and desk research and deliver a final report of their research to City staff. It is an ideal position for college students aged 18 or older, or anyone interested in local government and environmental work. The Piedmont Evergreen Program aims to increase recycling and composting throughout the city and reduce waste to the landfill. In the last several years, the city installed a three-can series of receptacles (waste, organics, and recyclables) to improve garbage diversion in public parks. Piedmont currently has a diversion rate of 75%, meaning that 75% of waste is composted or recycled, while 25% goes to the landfill, explained Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. The City’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 outlines the City’s goal to divert 85% of waste going to the landfill by 2030. To reach this goal and encourage further diversion, the City purchased additional waste, organic, and recycling receptacles for use in public areas throughout Piedmont. Responsibilities Volunteers will be expected to complete the following during the course of the project: • Bin Inventory: Complete a walking audit of Piedmont parks and other public places to locate and inventory all of the trash, recycling, and compost bins in the City. pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 3 PPD Officer Jason Germano saves man, dog from burning car By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont Police officer Jason Germano assisted Oakland police officers in rescuing a man and dog from a burning car on the city border on June 15. Officer Germano was on patrol when he heard on his radio that Oakland police needed help from someone with a fire extinguisher. A car was engulfed in flames at the intersection of Park Boulevard and Estates Drive on the Oakland-Piedmont border, and someone was still inside the vehicle. Germano arrived at the scene at about 11:20 p.m. “I grabbed my extinguisher from my vehicle and sprayed the front of the [crashed] car but wasn’t able to put the fire out,” he explained. Germano, an auto mechanic for over 20 years prior to joining the Police Department in 2019, said he understood that he had “limited time to act.” The driver initially refused to come out of the vehicle and appeared incoherent. Body camera footage shows Germano pulling the man out with the help of Oakland police officers. An OakBody camera footage shows the hood of the car engulfed in flames. Officer Jason Germano land officer then safely pulled the dog out of the burning vehicle. articles.text: Can you remember catching your young child in a lie? For most of us, this experience strikes fear: am I raising a deceitful person? Is this the first step down a dangerous path of dishonesty? Actually, lying is a normal part of cognitive-linguistic development which typically occurs during the preschool years. Studies show that up to 80% of 4-yearolds lie. This milestone indicates that the child has learned that other people have their own and often differing opinions. It signifies that the child has learned that they can use words in a more abstract way than simply to express their needs and wants, namely that words can get someone to think something that is not actually true. The child now understands that what we say does not always correspond with what we are thinking and sometimes we hide what we are really thinking and feeling. To make matters worse, this is often the age at which parents may start to encourage lying in certain situations, such as when they receive a present they already have or do not like. Fortunately, many positive traits are associated with this period of language development as well, such as increased communication related to conflict resolution, increased social competence and relationship building. The concomitant emergence of these skills will help parents when attempting to discuss this complicated topic with their little language learners. There are positive ways to talk to your toddler about lying. So, if we view the early appearance of lying as an important developmental milestone, rather than a morality issue, how can we best react to it? First, it is important to determine the function of the lie. Common functions include: to get something the child wants, to avoid embarrassment, to gain approval or attention, to remove the spotlight form themselves, to spare someone’s feelings, to avoid a consequence or conflict, or poor impulse control. Keeping the truth hidden or creating a “story” often makes the child feel better. Once we have determined the function of the lie, we can discuss it. Resist the impulse to ask, “why did you do that?” It is the first question parents go to, and unfortunately it does nothing to increase awareness or insight and adds the negative element of shame. Instead, stick to “what” and “how” questions to review what happened in a supportive and positive way. For example, you can ask what happened first, second, last. You can ask the child how they worked it out. You can discuss what the options were. You can talk about what the child can do differently next time. You can model what you would or would not have done in the situation. And lastly, postponing this kind of a discussion to a later time can allow for a more effective exchange and successful learning opportunity. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: Piedmont Boy Scouts Joseph Haggerty and Seamus Meagher of Troop 1 were presented with the rank of Eagle at a National Court of Honor on May 29 in the gardens at 212 Bonita Avenue among a crowd of family, friends, and fellow scouters. They were the 217th and 218th Scouts from Troop 1 to attain Scouting’s highest honor. Begun in 1920, Troop 1 is the Scouting unit in Piedmont. Both Haggerty and Meagher began their scouting journey in elementary school. They celebrated their Arrow of Light Ceremony together in March 2014. After visiting several troop open houses they settled on joining Troop 1 and have been a dynamic duo in the troop ever since, culminating in both earning the coveted MacTavish Award, which recognizes outstanding scouts in Troop 1. They were both part of The Order of the Arrow, a leadership unit. As they grew in scouting, so did their responsibilities, leadership, and service roles and experiences. pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 7 SUMMER THOUGHTS Does lying come naturally? By Katie Penguilly Can you remember catching your young child in a lie? For most of us, this experience strikes fear: am I raising a deceitful person? Is this the first step down a dangerous path of dishonesty? Actually, lying is a normal part of cognitive-linguistic development which typically occurs during the preschool years. Studies show that up to 80% of 4-yearolds lie. This milestone indicates that the child has learned that other people have their own and often differing opinions. It signifies that the child has learned that they can use words in a more abstract way than simply to express their needs and wants, namely that words can get someone to think something that is not actually true. The child now understands that what we say does not always correspond with what we are thinking and sometimes we hide what we are really thinking and feeling. To make matters worse, this is often the age at which parents may start to encourage lying in certain situations, such as when they receive a present they already have or do not like. Fortunately, many positive traits are associated with this period of language development as well, such as increased communication related to conflict resolution, increased social competence and relationship building. The concomitant emergence of these skills will help parents when attempting to discuss this complicated topic with their little language learners. There are positive ways to talk to your toddler about lying. So, if we view the early appearance of lying as an important developmental milestone, rather than a morality issue, how can we best react to it? First, it is important to determine the function of the lie. Common functions include: to get something the child wants, to avoid embarrassment, to gain approval or attention, to remove the spotlight form themselves, to spare someone’s feelings, to avoid a consequence or conflict, or poor impulse control. Keeping the truth hidden or creating a “story” often makes the child feel better. Once we have determined the function of the lie, we can discuss it. Resist the impulse to ask, “why did you do that?” It is the first question parents go to, and unfortunately it does nothing to increase awareness or insight and adds the negative element of shame. Instead, stick to “what” and “how” questions to review what happened in a supportive and positive way. For example, you can ask what happened first, second, last. You can ask the child how they worked it out. You can discuss what the options were. You can talk about what the child can do differently next time. You can model what you would or would not have done in the situation. And lastly, postponing this kind of a discussion to a later time can allow for a more effective exchange and successful learning opportunity. articles.text: The journey to this point in our life has been a long, ever twisting, roller coaster ride. Throughout the three years students have spent at Piedmont Middle School, we have gone through a great calamity that has forced us from the physical world, to the online world for our learning. And today we have gathered, undeterred. Despite every curve ball, every hurdle, every crazy thing thrown at us through these times, we are able to stand here today, permanently united, teacher and student alike. And as we close off this chapter for students, and move onto the next one, we only have one way to go from here, forward. With this, a new horizon has taken shape. Where, for the most part, the clouds have cleared, and the sun shines bright. The road ahead of us, all of us, is windy, and warped, with no clear sense of direction. It’s filled with potholes and road bumps. But alas, we cannot take a single step back. As deranged as this new coming world ahead of us may be, we have nowhere to go but permanently forward. We must keep our heads high; our will’s shining; to hold the eternal flame of life with us, as we continue down the road. Now, I want to bring out a single term popularized by Salvador Allende of Chile that I feel is related to this speech: Venceremos. What does this mean? “Let Us Triumph.” For as we move along with the infinite march of time, that is all we can strive for. The triumph of yourself, your friends, your community as a whole, triumph in the face of adversity. And with that, I wish all students and faculty of Piedmont Middle School a happy graduation. Let us triumph.

articles.text: School is out and summer is here. While kids are enjoying a well-deserved respite from “busy work,” it’s important to have a few summer activities that engage their senses and test their skills. Here is a great activity for elementary school-aged children, from kindergarten to 4th grade, that takes only minimal work by parents while still keeping them busy. Summer sensory station (ages 2 - 8) Sensory stations are easy to create and are tons of fun. They help develop vital skills in little ones, including fine motor skills, creativity, imagination and exploration. By adding items that encourage toddlers to stir, scoop, dig, and pour, you are providing opportunities to increase hand strength in your child. For older kids, about age 5, you can introduce items like tweezers, spoons, and funnels, tools that help them grasp patterns needed for handwriting and managing utensils. Sensory bins are also a quiet activity which allows children to calm down and play independently - the perfect “wind-down-before-nap time” activity. You can change your sensory bin however you’d like. First, grab a big plastic bin that will not leak. Then, choose your ‘base’ appropriately for your child’s age. Sand and water in a Choose an appropriate base for your bin. Water is a popular base for young, elementary aged children. Sensory bins are not just independent activities. Young kids will learn how to cooperate and take turns when playing together. shallow bin are perfect for toddler-aged kids. Don’t forget to add some food coloring or glitter in the water! For older kids, you can use aquarium rocks, twigs and leaves found outside, dry rice, pasta, or beans. Add in items like spoons, paper clips, tongs, mini spatulas, or any other tools children can use for play. Hiding dice, Scrabble pieces, or other number and letter shapes in the bin will provide children the opportunity to learn the alphabet, their numbers, and gain practice counting and spelling; talking with your child about the hidden items allows them to expand their vocabulary. articles.text: New Science Fiction and Fantasy – a sense of belonging The Post is publishing installments of The Best Books for Your Summer Reading List from the New York Times. Each list covers a handful of selections in genres such as Romance, Historical Fiction, Audio Books, and Thrillers. This assemblage includes Science Fiction, from a collection of short stories in translation, to a debut about a single consciousness in multiple bodies, to an Antarctic ghost story. The descriptions and reviews are edited for length. to do with the personalities of the individuals involved. Chaos on Catnet by Naomi Kritzer (Tor Teen, 292 pp.) Chaos introduces new characters and a dark mirror to Cheshire Cat, the friendly sentient artificial intelligence who loves pictures of cats and helping people make friends on the internet. This young-adult novel managed to be both a fantastic thriller and a phenomenally warm and kind bildungsroman. Kritzer’s author’s note at the end is well worth reading, both in its own right and as context for the book’s truncation. “One of the interesting things about near-future science fiction is that sometimes you catch up to the future while you’re still writing it,” she says, before addressing the reality of revising a book in the Twin Cities while Minneapolis was on fire during mass protests and a pandemic. Sorrowland by Rivers Solomon (MCD/Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 355 pp.) Sorrowland is a tremendous, riveting work, sinking long, deep roots into the nightmare soil of American history in order to grow and feed something new. It is concerned with the haunting weight of history and its effects on queer Black bodies; it reckons, through a fantastical lens, with inherited traumas and the consolations and difficulties of building community. Sorrowland’s patient, roiling intensity is as defiant and devastating as its heroine. Unity by Elly Bangs (Tachyon, 289 pp.) Unity f lings us hundreds of years into a future that has weathered multiple apocalypses and is on the brink of an extinction-level war between political powers that operate from metropolises beneath the much-warmed Pacific. Danae and her lover, Naoto, decide to risk heading for the blasted, inhospitable remnants of Arizona in search of the power and absolution of her whole, multiplied self. “Unity” is an astonishing debut, twisty and startling, demonstrating both the disciplined development of a long-gestated project and the raw, dynamic flashes of an author’s early work. In the opening story a groom and a bride’s struggle to meet each other at the correct time and place in order to marry, despite the vagaries of interstellar travel and relativity. pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 9 New York Times Summer Reading Lists New Science Fiction and Fantasy – a sense of belonging The Post is publishing installments of The Best Books for Your Summer Reading List from the New York Times. Each list covers a handful of selections in genres such as Romance, Historical Fiction, Audio Books, and Thrillers. This assemblage includes Science Fiction, from a collection of short stories in translation, to a debut about a single consciousness in multiple bodies, to an Antarctic ghost story. The descriptions and reviews are edited for length. SCIENCE FICTION Folklorn by Angela Mi Young Hur (Erewhon Books, 408 pp.) In many way Folklorn is also about translation: translation as physical movement, from Korea to the United States to Sweden to Antarctica; secret knowledge translated across languages and time; and translation as interpretation across genres, from folk tales and family history to experimental physics and poetry. Elsa is determined to choose science over superstition, but while researching neutrinos – so-called ghost particles – in Antarctica, she succumbs to an old hallucination of ringing bells and a lovely, mysterious woman with red ribbons trailing from her long black braid. Folklorn loops in and out of itself like a ghost’s red-ribboned braids, like a woman’s voice harmonizing with its own echoes. It’s beautiful and hard and hungry, full of sharp, painful observations, slicing clichés open like prickly pears and devouring their hearts. We are Satellites by Sarah Pinsker (Berkley, 381 pp.) Explores the far-reaching social implications of a new technology while staying deeply rooted in the day-to-day dynamics of a single family. In the novel, students show up at school with small blue lights embedded in their temples; they’ve chosen to have a productivity-boosting device called a Pilot installed in their brains, allowing them to achieve a state “as close to actual multitasking as a person can currently get.” The faultlines along which the family fractures have nothing to do with the presence or absence of shared DNA, and everything to do with the personalities of the individuals involved. Chaos on Catnet by Naomi Kritzer (Tor Teen, 292 pp.) Chaos introduces new characters and a dark mirror to Cheshire Cat, the friendly sentient artificial intelligence who loves pictures of cats and helping people make friends on the internet. This young-adult novel managed to be both a fantastic thriller and a phenomenally warm and kind bildungsroman. Kritzer’s author’s note at the end is well worth reading, both in its own right and as context for the book’s truncation. “One of the interesting things about near-future science fiction is that sometimes you catch up to the future while you’re still writing it,” she says, before addressing the reality of revising a book in the Twin Cities while Minneapolis was on fire during mass protests and a pandemic. Sorrowland by Rivers Solomon (MCD/Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 355 pp.) Sorrowland is a tremendous, riveting work, sinking long, deep roots into the nightmare soil of American history in order to grow and feed something new. It is concerned with the haunting weight of history and its effects on queer Black bodies; it reckons, through a fantastical lens, with inherited traumas and the consolations and difficulties of building community. Sorrowland’s patient, roiling intensity is as defiant and devastating as its heroine. Unity by Elly Bangs (Tachyon, 289 pp.) Unity f lings us hundreds of years into a future that has weathered multiple apocalypses and is on the brink of an extinction-level war between political powers that operate from metropolises beneath the much-warmed Pacific. Danae and her lover, Naoto, decide to risk heading for the blasted, inhospitable remnants of Arizona in search of the power and absolution of her whole, multiplied self. “Unity” is an astonishing debut, twisty and startling, demonstrating both the disciplined development of a long-gestated project and the raw, dynamic flashes of an author’s early work. Folklorn by Angela Mi Young Hur was published earlier this year. Rivers Solomon’s Sorrowland is a tremendous, riveting work. I’m Waiting for You: And Other Stories by Elizabeth Lippman (Harper Voyager, 316 pp.) A collection of four stories (two pairs of linked stories) translated from the Korean by Sophie Bowman and Sung Ryu. In the opening story a groom and a bride’s struggle to meet each other at the correct time and place in order to marry, despite the vagaries of interstellar travel and relativity. The iterations take place in a cosmic Dark Realm that contains our universe, and is populated by entities that regard Earth as a school in which to experience embodiment. This is a book as much about the process of translation as it is about science fiction, Buddhism and how to live among people. articles.text: Photos courtesy of ATPTour.com Mackie McDonald reached the first round of Wimbledon after winning three rounds in the qualifiers but lost in the opening round to Karen Khachanov in four sets. Former Piedmont resident Mackie McDonald suffered a first-round loss at the Wimbledon Championships on Monday, June 28, falling in four sets to No. 25 seeded Karen Khachanov of Russia, 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-6 (7-3). McDonald, No. 108, entered the first round as the heavy underdog to the 6-foot, 6-inch Khachanov, who is ranked No. 29 in the world. To reach the first round, McDonald entered as the No. 2 seeded player for the qualifiers at Wimbledon Park after beating Belgium’s Kimmer Coppejans 6-7 (7-5), 7-5, 6-2 on June 22, Ukraine’s Illya Marchenko 6-1, 3-6, 6-4 on June 23, and beating his former UCLA teammate, Maxime Cressy (ranked 152) in a five-set thunderous comeback on June 24, 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4. The loss to Khachanov, in the first round marked his third consecutive loss to a Top-25 opponent at a Grand Slam tournament since defeating Borna Coric in the Australian Open in February, Coric was ranked No. 24 when McDonald beat him 6-4, 6-2, 4-6, 6-4. Against Khachanov, McDonald opened strongly with a 6-3 victory in the first set but struggled to close out winnable games throughout, converting just three of 17 break point opportunities. In the three wins leading up to his match with Khachanov, McDonald was able to successfully hit his first serves to over 70 percent success rates. However, he had 61 percent of his first attempts in against the Russian. 5-Set win vs. Cressy The match with Cressy was UCLA teammates’ first match on the ATP tour. It featured Mackie rallying back from down two sets after losing 6-3, 6-4 to open before closing out with wins of 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, taking advantage of Cressy’s nine double faults while converting 71 percent of his first serves.

Luke Barrett, a 2020 Piedmont grad, recently completed his freshman year at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. LUKE BARRETT Basketball My goals for the summer are to build lower body and core strength. How are you measuring your development? I am tracking my weight, quickness, and overall strength in each workout. articles.text: Mathieu van der Poel holds Yellow Jersey through Stage 4 The 108th edition of the Tour de France is underway with Dutchman Mathieu van der Poel leading the general classification standings with an eight second advantage over Julian Alaphilippe of France through Stage 4. This year’s Grand Tour started at Brest in northeast France on June 26, the first day of a 3,417-kilometer route ending at the Avenue des Champs-Élysées on July 18. The Grand Départ from Brest started in a big way, but not for reasons typically expected. The race went viral during Stage 1 when a woman held out a sign as a greeting for her grandparents. It read “ALLEZ OPIOMI!” But standing too far onto the course with her back turned to the approaching peloton, she obstructed German cyclist Tony Martin, who collided with the fan and set off a domino effect of crashing riders. articles.text: Diego Rivera’s colossal mural, “Pan American Unity”, was moved from City College (pictured) to SFMOMA, where it was officially unveiled on June 28. On June 17, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco, “Pan American Unity”, was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. The priceless 4,000-pound series of panels, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together. The entire mural weighs nearly 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from Treasure Island after the World Exposition ended. It is the largest of the artists’ works and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the college’s theater, which is named for the artist. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to SF MOMA, where it officially went on display on June 28. “Diego was building a metamorphic bridge between the Mexican culture and the tech culture of the United States,” said Will Maynez, the former physics lab manager at City College. Maynez became a de facto guardian of the piece and “long dreamed of finding a way to allow more people to experience it.” He has spent 25 years researching and promoting “Pan American Unity.” Neal Benezra, SFMOMA Director, said, “This is one of the most ambitious things the museum has ever done — to move something this large, this fragile, and this important.” “We’re living in a time of tremendous resurgent nationalism around the world, and this is an anti-nationalist way of looking at things,” Benezra told The New York Times.

The Cabrillo Festival of Contemporary Music, America’s longest-running festival of new orchestral music and located in Santa Cruz, returns this summer with an all-virtual season over two weekends. Festival highlights include world premieres by composers Gabriela Lena Frank, Sean Shepherd, and Jake Heggie. The festival’s virtual season is completely free to the public and features dance, photography, videography, animation, and other art forms. Guest artists include the St. Lawrence String Quartet, mezzo-soprano Sasha Cooke, violinist Benjamin Beilman. This year, the award-winning Cabrillo Festival Orchestra will be led Cristian Macelaru. articles.text: Festival Opera’s 2021 season will continue at Piedmont Center for the Arts with a live-audience event on Sunday afternoon, July 11. “Un raggio di speme,” (“A Ray of Hope”) will be performed by Syrian-American coloratura soprano Lila Khazoum with celebrated pianist Alexander Katsman. The collection of songs is a celebration of the beauty of hope, even as it relates to loss and longing – a timely performance as we begin to gather again. The program also features virtuoso arias by Antonio Vivaldi, the tender storytelling in Sei ariette by Vincenzo Bellini, as well as the songs of George Bizet, Reynaldo Hahn, and Henri Duparc. This special event is the first concert presented at Piedmont Center for the Arts with a live audience since the onset of the COVID pandemic in March 2020. “I am thrilled by the opportunity to highlight this exciting new voice in the opera world with a live performance, and that we are making this performance available online to our friends around the globe,” said Festival Opera General Director, Zachary Gordin said. “Festival Opera maintains our commitment to seeking out and nurturing exceptionally talented artists and highlighting diverse voices. I look forward to this event with great excitement, and hope that you’ll join us either in person, or in the digital concert space.” The concert will begin at 5 p.m. Following the concert, a video interview with Khazoum and Gordin will be hosted on the organization’s YouTube channel. All ticket buyers will automatically receive a link to this companion offering. Soprano Lila Khazoum will appear at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on July 11. To purchase tickets, visit: https://www.festivalopera.org/ artist-recital-series

articles.text: As part of Cal Performances “Illuminations - Music and the Mind” programming, legendary soprano singer Renee Fleming presents a discussion and performance that is available to stream through July 28. Fleming performs with guest musicians and UC Berkeley Professor of Neuroscience Ehud Isacoff, as part of her own ongoing collaboration with educators and researchers. Fleming has explored the relationship between music and human psychology in her most recent work, and recently launched a live-streamed series of conversations and podcasts with leaders and practitioners working at the intersection of music, neuroscience, and healthcare. During next Thursday’s Soprano Renee Fleming performance, Fleming will offer insights into music’s potential for healing the mind, as well as perform illuminating selections from her repertoire with piano. Fleming is well-known for her performances in opera, concerts, recordings, theatre, and film around the world. Her signature roles include Countess Almaviva in Mozart’s Le nozze di Figaro, Desdemona in Verdi’s Otello, Violetta in Verdi’s La traviata, the title role in Dvorak’s Rusalka, and the title role in Massenet’s Manon. She is a recipient of the National Medal of Arts, and has been nominated for 17 Grammy awards throughout the span of her lengthy career. Beyond opera, she has recorded songs in jazz, musical theatre and independent rock. The stream is archived as part of Cal Performances “Performances at Home” series, which was created in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent venue closures. The video is available on demand until July 28. Visit https://secure.calperformances.org/15181/15820 for streaming information.

Therein is the essence and power of Just Mercy, a devastatingly good film that is understated while offering exceptional portrayals. The film is set in Alabama. The year is 1989. Walter McMillan (Jamie Foxx) is a black man on death row for a murder he could not possibly have committed. His conviction, as we learn, was based on the extorted testimony of a man (Tim Blake Nelson) who was known to be profoundly unreliable. And yet, as the record shows, there was no other physical evidence or witnesses produced by the prosecution that place McMillan at the scene. As we learn, there were multiple alibi witnesses who were ignored by the police and the D.A. And still McMillan was found guilty and sentenced by a judge who overturned the jury’s decision of life in prison and sentenced him to death by electrocution. When McMillan meets newly minted Harvard lawyer Bryan Stevenson (Michael B. Jordan), he has been on death row for six years and has exhausted countless avenues of appeal. He has lost all hope and concluded that he will die for a murder he did not commit. He initially rejects Stevenson’s offer of help. Undeterred, Stevenson begins to peel the evidentiary onion and is astonished to find that the state went ahead with what seems a prima facie case of an innocent man falsely accused, choosing instead to prosecute. Nevertheless, regardless of where Stevenson turns, he is met with a malevolent resistance by both the sheriff’s department and the local prosecutor. It’s at this point that Just Mercy becomes a legal procedural and a courtroom drama as Stevenson explores all alternatives open to him in an attempt to have all charges dropped, or, in the alternative, secure a new trial for McMillan. It is a harrowing process for Stevenson. He, like McMillan, is a black man who feels increasingly vulnerable and even threatened with harm. In one scene he is pulled over in the dead of night by the local police, a gun placed to the back of his head. He asks repeatedly why he was stopped and is braced, legs wide apart, against his car. The only words offered by the police are when he is told to get out of the car and called “boy” with a dripping malignancy. And yet both Stevenson and McMillan both refuse to abandon their belief that ultimately we are a nation of laws and that justice can prevail. The audience is not so certain. Just Mercy. Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton. Starring Michael B. Jordan, Jamie Foxx, Brie Larson. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated PG-13. Jamie Foxx plays Walter McMillian in Just Mercy.

By Chris Honoré Call it a staple of Hollywood screenwriting: girl meets damaged boy. She is moved to reach out and care for him, perhaps rescue him in some fashion. Ditto for boy meets damaged girl. Incrementally and inextricably, both scenarios become matters of the heart and love is soon entangled with the impulse to help. As stories go, it’s instantly familiar but also ripe with new and interesting permutations. Adam, written and directed by Max Mayer, is such a narrative. Beth (Rose Byrne), twenty-something, an aspiring writer of children’s books, having just escaped a disastrous love affair, moves into an Upper West Side brownstone. Living in the building is Adam (Hugh Dancy), an electrical engineer who designs toys and is also consumed with origins of the universe. When they first meet, in the laundry room, it is inescapable that Adam’s affect and responses are different. He doesn’t respond to the normal cues of conversation. Beth is intrigued for Adam is also bright and direct and sincere. What she soon learns is that his quirkiness is caused by Aspergers Syndrome, a form of high functioning autism. Though she comes to understand how Adam’s Aspergers presents itself, she also recognizes a lovely human being. In slow motion she falls in love with him and he with her. Beth also comes to understand that an aspect of the syndrome (at least in Adam’s case) is an inability to feel empathy, or make straightforward contact, such as looking her in the eyes. Adam hears what others say, but he is unable to feel the subtext behind the words or detect humor or irony. What is said, he takes at face value, even if a sentence ends with a question mark. Still, Beth moves forward, slowly involving Adam in her life, introducing him to her parents and to her friends. It’s not easy for her or for Adam. Adam is a sweet movie, wonderfully acted, and, to Mayer’s credit, explores both characters. Clearly, it was tempting to make this Adam’s story; Mayer resisted. Hence, Beth’s ambivalence and personal qualities are nicely balanced with Adam’s struggles. As well, there’s a tangential story concerning Beth’s affluent parents (Amy Irving and Peter Gallagher): her father is on trial for embezzlement, the family uncertain if he will go to prison. Adam is a small nugget when compared to the decidedly shallow fare that is offered up during the summer. Mayer takes a decidedly obscure condition and treats it with insight and genuine humanity and creates a touching film that’s worth seeing. articles.text: Rose Byrn plays Beatrix Potter in Peter Rabbit. Peter Rabbit is loosely based on the iconic book by Beatrix Potter. This incarnation is a fast-paced, frenetic comedy starring, Peter (James Corden), dressed in his familiar blue coat. Always mischievous, he resides on a bucolic farm in the English countryside. He lives a relatively carefree life along with his siblings Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki), and Cotton-tail (Daisey Ridley). This cohort also includes cousin Benjamin Bunny (Colin Moody) and is looked after by the kindly painter, Bea (Rose Byrn). Meanwhile the denizens of the warren clash with farmer McGregor (Sam Neil) whenever they raid his vegetable garden. But in one veggie raid, with Mr. McGregor in hot pursuit, he unexpectedly collapses and fails to get up. Now in the absence of old Mr. McG, the clan discovers it has the run of the farm, all happily gorging on rows and rows of vegetables. That is until Mr. McGregor’s great-nephew, Thomas (Domhnall Gleeson), moves from London to take over the farm, rehab the aging cottage, all in preparation for a quick sale. Feeling out of his element, he plans a quick return to the city and there opens a toy store. But Peter, of course, has other plans and so he and his rabbit tribe set out to obstruct Thomas at every turn, intending to sabotage this city slicker’s efforts. Unexpectedly, for Peter and crew, Thomas doesn’t retreat but decides that he’s all-in and the battle is joined, despite the reality that he doesn’t know a rake from a hoe. And thus begins the rabbit vs. city boy scrum over the rights to feed on the veggie garden whenever they please. As it turns out it was old man McGregor who had captured Peter’s father and turned him into a stew. So with a score to settle, and a carrot in hand, Peter, becomes a committed rebel, leaning into battle against another McGregor. Meanwhile, Thomas confides in Bea, telling her he has a “rabbit problem.” Bea in contrast is on the side of the rabbits insisting they are harmless and just part of the local color. No matter their viewpoints, Thomas does find Bea to be very charming. And so the story goes, riotous at times, and rarely slowing down. Kids will definitely be entertained. Peter Rabbit. Directed by Will Glick. Using live action and CGI with voices/performances by James Corden, Faysai Bazzi,Rose Byrn and Doomhnall Gleeson. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. articles.text: Luca, the 24th animated feature from Pixar, opened absent a wide theater release, and is now streaming on Disney+. It is a coming-of-age story set in the Italian seaside village of Portorosso, on the sun-washed Riviera, a place of dreamy blues, soft oranges, and inviting yellows. The time is somewhere between the 50s and 60s. At the center of the tale is Luca Paguro (Jacob Tremblay), a restless tween-teen who is a sea monster. He lives with his extended sea monster family in an underwater world. There’s Daniela, his mom (Maya Rudolph); Lorenzo Paguro, his dad (Jim Gaffigan); Grandma Paguro (Sandy Martin); and Uncle Ugo (Sacha Baron Cohen). Plus Luca’s new best friend, also a sea monster, Alberto Scorfario (Jack Dylan Grazer). The interesting twist is that when Luca and Alberto venture on shore they turn into regular boys who look like everyone else. And it’s on land where they discover that though they were warned by their families that the town of Portorosso could be dangerous, the boys find it filled with interesting, eye-widening possibilities. The two set off on an irresistible adventure. They meet a cast of interesting characters to include a feisty girl, Giulia Marcovaldo (Emma Berman), and her good-hearted fisherman/cook father, Massimo Marcovaldo (Marco Barricelli). They enter an annual Vespa race, take countless Vespa rides around town, meet and confront the previous winner of the Vespa race medal, the town bully, Saverio Raimondo (Ercole Visconti). Along the way, they learn the meaning of true friendship. The animation is delightful, the palette of detail and colors extraordinary. And the filmmakers acknowledge the influence of the iconic Japanese Studio Ghibli and the creative genius of animator and storyteller Hayao Miyazaki. Luca is a wonderful, imaginative story that should engage a wide audience of kids who will find Luca, both the sea monster and the boy, compelling.

articles.text: Jeanine and Guy Saperstein in front of the Picasso Museum in Paris. Guy and Jeanine Saperstein, longtime residents of Piedmont, have decided to sell their home on Glen Alpine Road and relocate permanently to France. The 12,000-square-foot house, the most expensive listing in Piedmont, was constructed in 1930 by renowned architects Williams and Wastell. The English Country Tudor-style home has been impeccably maintained throughout the years and features a hand-carved floating staircase against a two-story leaded glass window in a dramatic foyer. The home also boasts an elevator, attic game room, ballroom, home theatre, separate carriage house, and three-car garage. Why the move? The life-altering decision to move permanently across the globe is the result of what the couple sees as the stark inequality in this country. “There are tremendous inequalities [in America] racewise and class-wise. Two senators per state means there will never be a real democracy, and I don’t see that changing in a long time,” Guy confessed. Both are longtime civil rights workers and philanthropists. Guy has been named one of “the 100 most influential lawyers in America” by the National Law Journal. In 2006, he helped write the “Real Security” plank of the Democratic Party’s New Directions for America, and in 2007, helped found the National Security and Foreign Policy New Ideas Fund, with funding from the Democracy Alliance. He also has been Co-Chair of the Democracy Alliance’s Strategy Group and was active in its National Security/Foreign Policy Group. “We’re perched on the edge of potential fascism,” Guy said of members of the Republican party questioning the legitimacy of the 2020 election. “Added to that, I’m not enamored by the constant threat of wildfires, earthquakes… Even if we weren’t going to Paris, I needed to rethink living in California altogether.” Jeanine offered that, as a lifelong educator and philanthropist, she “wanted to make the world a better place.” “But we tried with his career, and my work in education; we tried to do what we could. In Europe, countries don’t have a big philanthropic movement, because people support [one another.] For a long time [in America,] people told us ‘either love it or leave it,’ and now we’re leaving it,” she said with sadness. “National healthcare, parental leave… many of the things we’ve fought for, they already have [in France].” Guy explained that the couple is relocating to Paris for a number of positive reasons. “Every country has social problems, but France has 19 times fewer crimes of violence than America. It’s safe to walk the streets at night,” he said. “France has a real middle class, and far less disparities than the truly wealthy. There’s virtually no homelessness.” “And Paris is basically a socialist province,” he added. The travel opportunities from Paris are also a draw, Jeanine noted. Being “smack-in-the-middle” of Europe allows for quick trips anywhere across the continent. The couple is looking forward to “lingering in Paris cafes, visiting world-class museums, meeting new people and bumping into old friends.” Their son, Leon, a fashion photographer who lives in Piedmont with his wife and son, lived in Paris for 10 years. “They always wanted to go back,” Jeanine said with a smile, and explained their plan to move several family members piecemeal to Europe. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had tours of the Mountain View Cemetery in 2018 and 2019, but missed their visit last year because of the pandemic. With Dr. Ron Bachman as their tour guide, the walkers turned out in force on Wednesday, June 23, with 40 people on the tour. The cemetery had been closed to the public until recently because of the pandemic, and is now still only open on Wednesdays and Saturdays. This was Dr. Bachman’s first docent tour in over a year too, so he was pleased to see so many people. The walkers met in front of the entrance to the main Mausoleum which is just beyond the fountain in front of the cemetery’s main office. Dr. Bachman is a retired Kaiser pediatrician with an additional area of expertise in epidemiology. His knowledge of Mountain View Cemetery and California history is that of a professor. After a brief introduction, he told the group that if they were fully vaccinated he was comfortable with them not wearing masks during the tour. He also explained the Messenger RNA science behind the vaccines which made the walkers all the more comfortable. Dr. Bachman told the group that Mountain View is a 226- acre cemetery established in 1863 by a group of East Bay pioneers led by Samuel Merritt. At that time there were a few local cemeteries, but Merritt’s group wanted to create a truly beautiful space for the final resting places of the area’s growing and prosperous population. The association they formed still operates the cemetery today. They bought 200 acers of land for $3,000, and an additional 26 acres were later purchased from the original Blair Park. Mountain View was designed in 1864 by Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect of New York City’s Central Park and much of the University of California in Berkeley and Stanford University. Many of California’s important historical figures are buried at the cemetery, including five California governors. Early California senators and many UC Berkeley presidents and professors are also buried at Mountain View. Its first burial was in 1865, and there is a section with Civil War veterans whose remains were moved to the cemetery after their deaths. Currently there are between 175,000 and 200,000 people buried at Mountain View, which has room for an additional 200,000 graves. Dr. Bachman took the group to the back of the Mausoleum. To show them the Strangers Plot that was established in 1870 for people who could not afford burials. This included many Chinese immigrants who helped build the railroads and worked in the California gold mines. Dr. Bachman took some time to tell the story behind a large Egyptian pyramid that the walkers came to. See the also attached photo of Dr. Bachman and members of the group. It is the mausoleum of U.S. Senator William Gwin. He was a medical doctor, politician, and a senator from Mississippi and later California. He and John Frémont were California’s first US senators. He died in 1885 at a time when Egyptian archeology and motifs were very popular. The histories of prominent architects Bernard Mayfield and Julia Morgan, as well as many other notable people and cemetery events, were also shared by Dr. Bachman. There are many grandiose crypts in tribute to the wealthy at Mountain View. Dr. Bachman concluded his tour by pointing out a ridge section of the cemetery with a set of large, tall buildings and a view of the Bay and San Francisco. It is known as “Millionaires’ Row,” and houses the mausoleums of the early California “Big Four,” the influential businessmen who funded the Central Pacific Railroad – Leland Stanford, Collis Potter Huntington, Mark Hopkins, and Charles Crocker. They built the western portion of the transcontinental railroad during the middle and late 1860s, creating routes that crossed both the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada range. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: If you are a grandparent of a young child today, there’s a good chance that your now-adult child watched many episodes of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood when they were growing up. As Mister Rogers zipped up his cardigan and donned his house sneakers, he sang “It’s a beautiful day in the neighborhood...” while a little piano riff played in the background. Next, Mister Rogers fed the fish and then sat down, looked directly into the camera lens, and spoke directly to each individual young viewer, usually about feelings. He told each child: “I like you just the way you are.” Mister Rogers tackled the current events of the day by seeing the world through the eyes of a child and addressing the scary parts with the reassurance of a wise elder. The renewed interest in the teachings and the biography of Fred Rogers nearly two decades after his death in 2003 is extraordinary. It has spawned documentaries, biopics, podcasts, books, educational seminars, magazine articles, blogs, Facebook pages, and countless academic essays on the profound impact that he had on children’s educational television, and more importantly, on educating and guiding the adults who interact with small children. What can grandparents of young children learn from the legacy of Mister Rogers? Most grandparents have the luxury of not being in the role of primary guardian of small children with the requisite responsibilities for their education, health, nutrition, etc. This leaves room for possibly the most important role anyone (apart from a parent) may play in a child’s life: the person who can love the child just the way they are. “Knowing that we can be loved exactly as we are gives us all the best opportunity for growing into the healthiest of people.” Mister Rogers wanted adults to understand that ideally, we love others not because they are particularly good or particularly special, but rather, because we are all special and deserving of love, understanding, acceptance, and kindness. And he hoped that this lesson could be communicated to children. Mister Rogers taught us that we can love another person even if they are imperfect, or very different from ourselves, or even if we don’t really know them very well. articles.text: One year ago in April, while driving across the Bay Bridge it was hard to miss seeing the Grand Princess, the enormous white cruise ship docked in Oakland. The local news reported the story, but seeing it hit me hard. It was a ship full of vacationers, many of whom had COVID. It was international news. My phone started ringing with friends and family calling and texting who imagined the ship disembarking onto my neighborhood streets. None of us knew what was ahead. We hadn’t yet learned what we now know. And so, 2020 began a year of near-daily panic. A long, slow year marked by never-ending news stories of COVID, George Floyd’s death, homelessness, and the election. My spring birthday typically is marked by the usual seasonal changes, lush green California hills, the buzz of bees, and pretty, blooming trees. This year, spring has hit me with a jolt of self-reflection, digesting what I’ve been through, what we’ve all been through. It was not entirely traumatic; I never got COVID. I remember being in disbelief when at Safeway seeing only potatoes and onions in the produce section after Governor Newsom ordered the shelter in place. I drove home, sat down, and had my first panic attack. I often thought this past year about my parents who talked about the Depression during their lives. It stayed with them, as I’m pretty sure the pandemic will stay with all of us regardless of our ages. Today I’m more resilient than I ever imagined. I understand how to pivot. I’ve become a better bird watcher, gardener, wife, mother, and cook. I’ve learned how to stay in the moment. My life, along with everyone’s on the planet, slowed and returning to “normal” feels scary. I’m out of practice on almost all things. I wonder I we all could move forward getting back our lives slowly and rethinking almost everything. The pandemic put a spotlight on so many things, cracks in our society. How we treat our citizens. Who is in our safety net? It’s a question I keep asking myself. I’m weary, resilient, but finally fully vaccinated. Joanne Devereaux is a freelance writer and owner of Mindful Transitions, serving the needs of seniors and their families throughout the downsizing and home moving process. articles.text: The American Red Cross continues to experience a severe blood shortage. Blood and platelet donors are needed now to help ensure hospital shelves are stocked with blood products over the Fourth of July holiday and beyond. As a thank-you, all those who come to give July 1-6 will receive a Red Cross embroidered hat by mail. And donors who donate blood between July 7-31 will receive a $10 Amazon.com gift card by email, plus a chance to win gas for one year (a $5,000 value). Donors of all blood types – especially type O and those giving platelets – are urged to make an appointment to give now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood. org, or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767). The Red Cross is working around the clock to provide blood products to hospitals responding to an unusually high number of traumas and emergency room visits, as well as overdoses and resulting transplants. As a result of the blood shortage, some hospitals are being forced to slow the pace of elective surgeries until the blood supply stabilizes, delaying crucial patient care. To donate blood, call the Oakland Blood Bank, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 800-733-2767. The blood bank is open from 7:45 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. most days, and until 6:45 p.m. on June 30 and July 6. To donate blood, individuals need to bring a driver’s license or their blood donor card. Individuals aged 17 who weigh at least 110 pounds and are in good health may be eligible to donate blood.

articles.text: When someone needs assistance with daily activities in the home, it can appear that they never leave home. In some cases, due to a chronic illness, infection concerns, or mobility issues, a person may not be able to go out much. However, a professionally trained caregiver can become a companion outside of the home too and help with activities when away from home. Traveling by plane, car, or train can be complicated and require many stops along the way that require the assistance of a caregiver. Simply pausing for a bathroom break safely may necessitate help from someone else, while handling luggage and important papers too. Before embarking on a trip, stop to consider all of the little ways in which a caregiver helps around the house – daily or weekly. Then, weigh the risks of not having the caregiver along for a trip. Will there be walking and inherent fall risks? Are all bathrooms accessible with grab bars? Are medication reminders needed daily? A trusted caregiver with the proper training can be of help in these new settings and make a big trip more enjoyable as well as safe. Maybe taking a big trip is out of the question, but it is possible to leave the home for a short time with the help of a caregiver. This variety in the day can be meaningful for someone who’s activities have become limited as a result of age or illness. Not every outing with a caregiver has to be a chore, such as a trip to the grocery store or a visit to the doctor’s office. A caregiver can be there for a favorite neighborhood visit, a scenic drive, or a walk in a park – a time to be there when catching up with an old friend so that things go smoothly with food preparation or light housekeeping. Each of these experiences can be an opportunity to make new memories and break up mundane routines. This summer – or any time of year for that matter – consider doing something new outside the home with the support of a caregiver for yourself or a loved one who could benefit from new surroundings. pages.text: Wednesday, June 30, 2021 25 By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Readers: Buyer beware! Today’s article is about a situation I came across last week with a customer (whom I will call Andrew) who bought a new 21.5 inch iMac in January. Since he and his family are now fully vaccinated (as am I), I did a house call to set up this new machine. When I looked at the specs of the machine, we realized that this iMac was from 2017. I was not aware that these 21.5 inch iMacs have not been updated since then. Of course, Andrew was not happy, having bought this machine new from Apple. So, we called Apple’s sales department and were transferred to a representative in “post sales”. The agent declared that although the model has not been updated since 2017, the machine was built new in January. I told him that my client had not been informed of the age of the model he was purchasing. And that he had spent a long time talking to the sales representative, and indicated over and over again that he wanted a new machine. He explained that he was replacing an eight-year-old machine and wanted something that would last him for another eight years. They discussed the 21.5 inch versus the 27 inch, and because of space requirements my client chose the smaller. This client is an expert in many things, but technology is not one of them. He indicated to the sales person that he was really just concerned with getting something that would have the same longevity as his previous machine. Never in the conversation, did the sales person tell him that the iMac model he was buying, although new, was made up of components from 2017. So, thinking he would have another seven or eight years on this machine, Andrew ended up buying a fouryear old machine. I requested that my client be allowed to return this computer for a newer model, and of course the answer was this: “I’m so sorry, but you were outside the two week return window”. I said to the agent, of course we are, but with the pandemic, this was the first chance we have had to be together to do the set up. And I strongly suggested that the sales person was remiss in providing all the information necessary for my client to make a good decision. With sales in technology, it’s up to the sales person to explain to the consumer what in fact they are buying. The representative promised to send this to a higher tier, and someone in this mysterious department called Andrew later that day. The bottom line in the conversation with this representative was, “we are so sorry, there’s really nothing we can do.” Andrew called me and gave me the number of this mysterious department, and I called them the next morning. After being disconnected once, I finally spoke to a representative named Dawn. At first, she gave me the same company line, that this was outside the two-week return window. I stressed that those requirements should not be enforced during these times, when clients have not been able to get in-home support until now. I also stated to her many instances of what I would call “age-ism” with previous clients and with Andrew. And I stressed that with computer sales, it is up to the salesperson to explain to the consumer exactly what they are getting. I reminded her that Andrew was never told that he was getting a new build of a four-year old machine, and that had he been informed, he would have chosen a different model. I told her about a previous instance where a client went into one of the local Apple stores to buy a new machine. This client was a retired professor, who had had a stroke. His IQ was off the charts, a very bright man. His speech was affected by the stroke, and he had a little card printed up to give to salespeople to explain his situation. The last sentence on this card, which was just brilliant, was “I’m not stupid, I just talk funny.” This client was treated like a five-year-old child, and although he explained in writing on a note pad he kept that he takes a lot of photos, he was sold a laptop with a small hard drive with the lowest amount of RAM. When I was called to set it up, I promptly recommended he exchange it for a larger and faster machine. Again, had the representative listened to his needs, he would have recommended the appropriate machine. After talking for more than an hour, Dawn promised she would advocate for us and call me back. I explained to Dawn that we would not let this go if the response was in the negative and that we would call some consumer advocates, possibly the newspaper, possibly AARP. About 20 minutes later, she called me back and said that they would take this machine for a refund. She also indicated that the sales person was no longer working for Apple. I thanked her profusely and recommended that she tell her higher ups that they need to train their salespeople better to deal with customers of all ages. Here is a list of what Apple has for sale right now on their website and the release dates: • MacBook Air: Nov 2020 • 13-inch MacBook Pro Intel Model: May 2020 • 13-inch MacBook Pro Apple M1 Model: Nov 2020 • 16-inch MacBook Pro Intel Model: Nov 2019 • MacMini: Nov 2020 • 21.5-inch iMac (no longer on their site): June 2017 • 24-inch iMac: April 2021 • 27-inch iMac: Aug 2020 What can we take from this? When it is time to upgrade your computer, please remember to ask questions. If you are an artist, musician or photographer, you need processing speed and power as well as storage space if you want to store your media on the computer. If you are just emailing and surfing the web, you need a simpler setup. Remember to ask the production date of the model that is being recommended. And if you need buying advice, contact me. I’ll be happy to help. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com and themacmama.blogspot.com. The goats are a natural and rugged way to clear grasses and brush ‘ladder fuels’ which could carry fire from the ground into the trees,” explained Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “The goats can get to hardto-reach areas, work efficiently, and don’t use any fossil fuels once delivered to the location. “In addition, they are fun to watch,” he added with a grin. Annual vegetation management helps firefighters control a grass fire before it becomes a conflagration, Brannigan added, like the 1991 Oakland-Berkeley hills fire, or the more recent Tubbs Fire in Santa Rosa. The length of time the goats will be here depends entirely on the herd’s appetite, although they will need to be moved out of urban areas before Independence Day, because the sound of fireworks spooks them. The herd will eat their way around the open space surrounding the Corporation Yard. Once that area is cleared of dry brush, they will cross Moraga Avenue and eat the vegetation at Blair Park. “This could take a week, it could take two – we’ll see how fast the goats chew,” Brannigan said. The Piedmont Fire Department asks that residents who want to see the herd keep in mind not to park on dry grasses or block traffic. And although it may be tempting, do not try to touch the goats.
